content: Sodium selenate, with the chemical formula Na₂SeO₄, is a white, odorless solid that forms as the sodium salt of selenic acid. It should not be confused with sodium selenite. This compound was discovered shortly after the element selenium was identified by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1817. Initially, sodium selenate was used as a staining agent for glassware. Despite its high toxicity, it is commonly included in multivitamins and livestock feed as a source of selenium due to its high solubility and relatively low reactivity. Research into the biological effects of selenium has highlighted sodium selenate's regulatory role in the function of the protein phosphatase PP2A. This protein is crucial in angiogenesis and has been linked to cancer cell growth and the progression of Alzheimer’s disease. The primary method for isolating sodium selenate, patented in 1986, involves dissolving metallic selenium in nitric acid to produce selenous acid. This acid is then treated with an alkali metal hydroxide, carbonate, or other metal oxide/hydroxide to form an alkali metal selenite. The selenite is subsequently oxidized in a basic environment using hydrogen peroxide to form selenate, which is then spray-dried. One of the earliest industrial applications of sodium selenate was in glass manufacturing. Selenium imparts a red hue to glass, and sodium selenate is particularly effective due to its stability at high temperatures. When combined with arsenic trioxide, it reduces to elemental selenium, which complements the green hue caused by ferrous oxides, resulting in clear glass. Sodium selenate is also a common ingredient in insecticides targeting mites, aphids, and mealybugs, as well as in fungicides. A dose of 10 mg/kg is typically lethal for most insects. Initially valued for its glass-coloring properties, sodium selenate gained prominence in the 1950s when the biological role of selenium became more widely studied. It has since become a significant focus in oncological and neurological research. Recent studies have explored sodium selenate's role in regulating protein phosphatases, particularly PP2A, which dephosphorylates proteins involved in pro-angiogenic signaling. Angiogenesis, a key process in the growth and spread of malignant tumors, is regulated by protein kinases through reversible phosphorylation. Sodium selenate has been shown to stimulate PP2A effectively, disrupting pathways like PI3K/Akt and MAPK, which are critical to angiogenic signaling. In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), characterized by amyloid β plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles, sodium selenate has demonstrated the ability to reduce tau phosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo. It has also been shown to improve memory and motor performance while preventing neurodegeneration. Sodium selenate mitigates tau pathology by targeting PP2A, which is found at elevated levels in AD-affected brains. This compound is a promising lead in the treatment of AD and other forms of dementia, driving further research. Sodium selenate is a common ingredient in over-the-counter vitamin supplements due to its selenium content and high solubility. Selenium, though a trace element, is essential for health, and its deficiency has been linked to conditions such as heart disease, hyperthyroidism, and weakened immunity. Diseases like Keshan disease, Kashin-Beck disease, and myxedematous endemic cretinism are also associated with selenium deficiency. Conversely, excessive selenium intake can lead to selenosis, a condition characterized by symptoms such as gastrointestinal upset, hair loss, white blotchy nails, garlic breath odor, fatigue, irritability, and mild nerve damage. Selenosis occurs at blood selenium levels exceeding 100 µg/dL. Selenium deficiency in livestock has become a concern due to selenium-poor soil. Sodium selenate and selenite are commonly used in premixed animal feed, with no significant difference in selenium absorption between the two compounds. The FDA regulates selenium content in animal feed to a maximum of 5 ppm. In 2009, a controversy arose when 21 polo horses died from selenium poisoning due to a pharmacy error in mixing a dietary supplement, prompting a review of animal dietary requirements. The FDA and European Union classify sodium selenate as a toxic chemical, particularly if ingested or inhaled. A dose of 6 mg/kg is considered lethal, corresponding to 112 mg for a 70 kg individual, or 560 pills of 200 mcg each. Chronic exposure to sodium selenate can cause severe damage to the lungs, kidneys, and liver. Studies on its antigen properties and dosage have shown good tolerance at doses up to 45 mg per day, with a maximum tolerated dose of 60 mg per day. Side effects include nail disorders, alopecia, muscle spasms, and nausea. Higher doses may lead to increased side effects, such as nausea and fatigue, attributed to the accumulation of selenite.
